title: WHAT DELAYED MOSES FOR FORTY YEARS?
paragraphs: WHAT DELAYED MOSES FOR FORTY YEARS?
The desert was never supposed to be Moses’ destination.
It was only supposed to be a detour.
Yet the man who would one day stand before Pharaoh, split the Red Sea, receive the Law, and lead a nation into covenant with God spent forty years watching sheep.
Forty years.
Not forty days.
Not forty months.
Forty years.
For many believers, that number feels painfully familiar.
You know God called you.
You know there is more.
You know there are promises, assignments, opportunities, and purposes that seem written somewhere in your future.
Yet somehow, life feels stalled.
Years pass.
Dreams fade.
Prayers grow quieter.
And the question begins haunting the soul:
“What delayed Moses for forty years?”
The answer may reveal why so many of us remain in wilderness seasons longer than God originally intended.
The story begins in scandal.
Because God has always specialized in taking scandal and turning it into grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Moses was born under a death sentence.
Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys to be killed. Yet God preserved Moses through an unlikely chain of events involving a courageous mother, a basket floating among reeds, and Pharaoh’s own daughter.
From the beginning, God’s hand was unmistakably on his life.
Moses grew up in Egyptian royalty.
He had education.
Influence.
Resources.
Access.
Power.
Everything the world says is necessary for greatness.
But possessing a calling is not the same thing as being ready for it.
One day Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
Something erupted inside him.
Scripture says:
“When Moses was grown, he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens.” (Exodus 2:11)
He knew who he was.
He knew where he belonged.
He knew injustice when he saw it.
But what happened next would alter the next four decades of his life.
Moses killed the Egyptian.
The Hebrew text uses the verb וַיַּךְ (vayyakh), meaning “he struck” or “he smote.”
This was not merely self-defense.
This was Moses attempting to accomplish God’s purpose through human force.
The problem was not his burden.
The problem was his method.
Many believers make the same mistake.
God gives a vision.
We manufacture a timeline.
God gives a promise.
We create our own strategy.
God speaks.
We run ahead.
Then we wonder why doors close.
Moses believed the time had come.
But heaven had not yet said, “Go.”
The result was devastating.
His crime became known.
Pharaoh sought to kill him.
The prince became a fugitive.
The future deliverer became a shepherd.
The palace became a wilderness.
Acts 7:25 reveals something profound:
“For he supposed his brethren would have understood how God by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not.”
Moses was not confused about his calling.
He was confused about God's timing.
Those are not the same thing.
Many of the greatest frustrations in life are not caused by being outside God’s purpose.
They are caused by trying to fulfill God’s purpose before God’s preparation is complete.
The wilderness was not punishment.
The wilderness was training.
This changes everything.
Many people assume Moses wasted forty years.
Scripture suggests God was shaping him.
Egypt taught Moses how to be a prince.
Midian taught Moses how to be a servant.
Egypt taught him authority.
Midian taught him dependence.
Egypt taught him confidence.
Midian taught him humility.
And God cannot entrust spiritual authority to a heart that has not learned surrender.
The irony is astonishing.
The man who once believed he could rescue Israel by killing one Egyptian would eventually lead millions by trusting God instead of himself.
The desert stripped away the illusion of self-sufficiency.
That process took time.
Far more time than Moses probably wanted.
Far more time than we usually want.
In Hebrew thought, the wilderness carries profound symbolism.
The Hebrew word is מִדְבָּר (midbar).
Interestingly, it shares linguistic roots connected to speech and word.
Many Jewish scholars have observed the connection between wilderness and divine communication.
The place that appears empty often becomes the place where God speaks most clearly.
How many believers can testify to that reality?
It was not in success that they heard Him most clearly.
It was not during applause.
It was not during promotion.
It was during heartbreak.
Failure.
Waiting.
Silence.
Wilderness.
That is where God's voice became unmistakable.
Then one ordinary day changed everything.
Moses was eighty years old.
Eighty.
Most people would have considered their greatest opportunities behind them.
Yet God was only beginning.
A bush burned without being consumed.
And from the flames came the voice of God.
In Exodus 3:14, God revealed His covenant name:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh.
Often translated:
“I AM WHO I AM.”
More literally:
“I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
God was revealing His eternal self-existence.
His faithfulness.
His sovereignty over time itself.
The God who speaks from the burning bush is not limited by delayed dreams, missed opportunities, aging bodies, broken histories, or wilderness years.
Nothing is late when God is involved.
Nothing.
The years Moses thought were lost were not lost at all.
God was writing a bigger story.
The same truth echoes throughout Scripture.
Joseph endured prison before the palace.
David endured caves before the crown.
Paul endured obscurity before global ministry.
Even Jesus spent approximately thirty years in preparation before three years of public ministry transformed history forever.
God is never in a hurry.
Because God sees the whole story.
We only see the chapter.
Perhaps the greatest delay in Moses’ life was not geographical.
It was internal.
God had to remove Egypt from Moses before Moses could lead Israel out of Egypt.
And sometimes God must remove things from us before He can release us into what He promised.
Pride.
Self-reliance.
Bitterness.
Fear.
Control.
Hidden idols.
False identities.
The wilderness exposes what prosperity often conceals.
That can feel painful.
But it is grace.
Because the God who wounds also heals.
The God who convicts also restores.
The God who disciplines also redeems.
The cross proves this forever.
When Jesus cried from Calvary:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
He declared the complete accomplishment of redemption.
Every wilderness.
Every failure.
Every regret.
Every delay.
Every scandal.
Every broken chapter.
Every wasted year surrendered to Christ can be rewritten by grace.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Moses' story was never ultimately about Moses.
It pointed forward to a greater Deliverer.
Jesus Christ.
Moses led people through a sea.
Jesus leads people through death into life.
Moses delivered people from slavery to Pharaoh.
Jesus delivers people from slavery to sin.
Moses brought God's law.
Jesus fulfilled God's law.
Moses reflected God's glory.
Jesus is God's glory.
The wilderness was not the end of Moses’ story.
And your wilderness is not the end of yours.
Perhaps the question is not:
“Why has God delayed me?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“What is God producing in me while I wait?”
Because waiting is not wasted when God is working.
Maybe you have spent years carrying disappointment.
Maybe prayers remain unanswered.
Maybe promises seem distant.
Maybe life looks nothing like what you imagined.
Take heart.
The God of the burning bush still speaks.
The God who called Moses still calls ordinary people.
The God who redeemed Moses' failure still redeems failures today.
And the God who transformed a murderer into a deliverer still transforms lives through Jesus Christ.
If this article stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Sometimes one shared message becomes the encouragement that changes an entire life.
Your testimony may become someone else's breakthrough.
Return to it whenever you need the reminder that God is still writing your story.
Because somewhere right now, another Moses is sitting in a wilderness wondering if God has forgotten him.
And maybe your share is the burning bush God uses to remind him He has not.
The wilderness was never where Moses was buried.
It was where Moses was built.
